mainEntity.name: What is the Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue Test?

acceptedAnswer.text: It’s a recognised assessment of hue discrimination . You arrange coloured tiles so they transition smoothly from one hue to another. A higher score means better colour perception.

mainEntity.name: Why does colour perception matter for photographers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Editing, colour grading and printing all depend on accurate hue recognition. Weak hue perception can lead to subtle but persistent casts (too warm/cool or magenta/green) that look unnatural in skin tones, foliage and prints.

mainEntity.name: How do I read my score?

acceptedAnswer.text: 90–100 = excellent; 75–89 = good; 60–74 = moderate (take extra care with WB/tint); below 60 = limited — use neutral lighting, reference targets and second-pair-of-eyes checks.

mainEntity.name: Do I need special equipment to take the test?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use a desktop or laptop with a mouse . Mobile devices aren’t supported. View in neutral light and avoid screen night-shift modes to prevent colour bias.

mainEntity.name: Can I compensate for weaker colour perception?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes: shoot a grey card, edit under neutral lighting (5000–6500K), use reference images, make small A/B adjustments, calibrate your monitor, and get feedback on tricky colour work.
